title: Adaptive KV-cache companding and low-bit quant experiments
creator: Sofia Patel
description: Goal: evaluate perceptual and n-gram quality trade-offs of compressed KV caches using FP8/INT8/INT4 representations with adaptive companding and progressive fallback strategies. We want to reduce GPU memory for long-context workloads (>= 16k tokens) while keeping generation quality and latency within product SLOs. This ticket coordinates the experiment harness, model variants, dataset selection, evaluation metrics, and rollout safety checks.
approach: 1) Implement layer-wise quantization hooks in the KV cache serializer that support per-head scaling and companding (log-scale + learned bias). 2) Add progressive compression modes: (a) lossless FP16 baseline, (b) FP8 dynamic, (c) INT8 calibrated, (d) INT4 aggressive with per-channel scale. 3) Integrate a runtime fallback policy: if a rollout route observes top-k token divergence beyond threshold or perplexity delta > X, automatically rehydrate affected prefixes in FP16. 4) Measure interaction with continuous batching and eviction policy: evaluate how compressed KV cache affects cache hit latency and batch assembly times.
experiment_plan: Implement quant codec in runtime: CPU-side encode/decode + GPU fast path using fused kernels
Run microbenchmarks for encode/decode latency across common sequence lengths (512, 2048, 8192, 16384)
Run quality evals on held-out prompt sets: summarization (CNN/DailyMail subset), long-form Q&A (EVALS-LONG-2k+), and code completion (HumanEval-like long-context prompts)
Collect metrics: token-level divergence, perplexity, ROUGE, exact-match for QA, pass@k for code, latency P50/P95, GPU mem savings per model, and occurrence of hallucination indicators
A/B test canary on small dedicated capacity pool with synthetic traffic to validate runtime stability and throughput before broader rollout
results_summary: Early microbenchmarks (FP8/INT8) show 30-38% reduction in KV memory footprint and ~5-12% additional end-to-end latency due to encode/decode on CPU path when sequences < 2k. For long contexts (>=8k), GPU-only decode kernel reduces overhead and total latency impact falls to <3%. Quality: FP8 preserved perplexity within +0.6% on average; INT8 showed +1.9% delta; INT4 caused visible degradation on instruction-following prompts and increased token divergence in tail generation. Notable regression: INT4 increased hallucination-like factual errors on long-context QA in ~2.4% of prompts compared to FP16 baseline.

analysis_notes: Key technical observations and hypotheses: 1) Per-channel scaling with a small residual bias reduces INT4 outliers on rare-token attention heads. 2) Progressive companding (log-space then linear) helps preserve dynamic range for very long prefixes. 3) Encode on CPU is acceptable at high batch sizes but hurts p95 for low-batch interactive traffic; plan to offload encode to an async GPU kernel or overlap encode with compute. 4) Continuous batching pipeline must be aware of compressed cache sizes to avoid assembling batches that exceed memory despite per-request savings.
